Korea’s last major dynasty, the kingdom of Joseon (1392-1897 CE) saw the House of Yi ruling the peninsula (albeit as a tributary state of Ming and Qing) for over five hundred years. Described as “the hermit kingdom” owing to its isolation and self-reliance, Joseon was a point of stability through the high era of colonialism, a bastion of Confucianism, and a difficult target for would-be invaders. In a world that seemed to be crumbling around them, Koreans in Joseon sought a firm footing – and a path forward.

In the last years of the 14th century, China was at a turning point, as the Mongol-led Yuan court was collapsing and the new Ming Dynasty was seeking to find its own footing. In the chaos, Goryeo, a former vassal of Yuan, asserted its claim to ancient lands in Manchuria. But not all Koreans were happy about standing alone against the rising Ming. General Yi Song-gye saw an opportunity for a new, more peaceful future order for East Asia. He disobeyed orders to march on the Ming and instead turned his armies around, seizing the Goryeo capital and founding a new Korean dynasty. This was Joseon, and General Yi took the name Taejo upon becoming king.

In this early period, Joseon was a tributary of Ming but retained a good deal of independence. The kingdom saw the codification and flourishing of Korean culture, especially under Sejong the Great (r. 1418-1450), who developed Hangul, the writing system Koreans still use today, and sought to bring Neo-Confucian ethics into an organizing principle of Korean life. Groups of politically powerful Confucian scholars – the sarim – earned their right to participate in court life via meritocratic study and set the stage for a hybrid form of monarchical rule and meritocratic bureaucracy.

This early Joseon period was to face its greatest challenge from outside the kingdom, twice. In 1592, Japan attempted an invasion as a beachhead to a further invasion of Ming China but was eventually repelled. But Ming was to fall regardless. In 1636, the newly established Qing invaded Joseon, and after a devastating war, Joseon became a tributary state of the new Qing Dynasty. But despite this dependency, Joseon revered the lost Ming, and preserved much of its Confucian ideals. In becoming more inward-focused, it still thrived. In this time of peace, isolation, and Confucian study, Joseon enters our Modern Age.

Though the American writer William Elliot Griffis termed modern-era Joseon “the hermit kingdom” owing to its policies of isolation, this was not entirely accurate. Rather, the Joseon elites sought to negotiate the terms of their own openness. Silhak scholars – a newer school of Confucian thought focused on practical knowledge – advocated for a philosophy of the “Eastern Way and Western Instruments” (dongdo seogi ron), adopting Western technology while retaining Korean religion and Confucian governance in order to gain the prosperity of the Western powers without losing the Korean soul.

Joseon society was strictly hierarchical, with four distinct classes of people and everyday life governed under Confucian law. Class and gender structure was strict, with enslaved people (until 1800) under commoners, who in turn were under the “middle people,” who in turn were under the nobility. In Joseon, one always had a place. In practice, Joseon was an absolute monarchy, but the Joseon monarchy saw itself as a part of society, aiming to be a balancing force and cooling the divisive struggles between factions.

This internal balance and relatively hands-off status vis-à-vis Qing gave rise to a stable calm. Joseon’s armies and navies were quiescent, and its civil society carefully controlled, but prosperous. But in the late 19th century, new tensions began to rise. With Qing weakened by war with Japan, Korea declared independence – and imperial status. The Empire of Korea marks the end of Joseon as well as a brief flash of Korean independence. But Russia and Japan were not done with their contest over control of Northeast Asia, and both sought to claim Korea for their own. As Japanese imperialism rose at the end of late Meiji, Korea was annexed into the Japanese Empire in 1910 and remained under Japanese control until the end of World War II.

King Jeongjo (r. 1776-1800) was one of the most significant of Joseon’s monarchs, reforming Joseon society and modernizing its military. Key among these modernizations was the construction of Hwaseong Fortress, a massive bastion built between 1794 and 1796 as a monument to Jeongjo’s cruelly murdered father. It is an impressive structure, containing multiple walls and crossbow stations, secret gates and lookout towers, and would have been a nearly impregnable structure. None dared to take it during Joseon, a testament to the relative peace of Joseon as much as to its defenses, and it remained a place for military organization as well as a site for Jeongjo to visit the remains of his father.

Hwaseong did see conflict, though, during the Korean War in the middle of the 20th century, when tanks burned in the shadow of crossbow stations. It remains an important monument to Joseon life today.

Distinguished from the private seowon, the hyanggyo were government-run Confucian schools that were present in every community in Korea. They aimed to educate the children of yangban – nobility – in preparation for civil exams, but were not the theoretical and political powerhouses that seowon came to be. Nonetheless, they were responsible for keeping the Korean upper classes literate and focused on a meritocratic order.

Korea has had a long history of printing using moveable metal type. This technology originated in Goryeo, where the Jikji, a collection of Seon (Zen) monks’ accounts and the oldest extant printed book, was printed in 1377. But printing in Joseon became vital to state rule. As the dominant religion in Korea moved towards Confucianism, printing houses became ways for rulers to disseminate Confucian and other cultural ideas, standardizing and mass-producing sermons that could then be distributed to officials, and helping to unify and standardize Joseon rule.

Confucianism defined the culture of Joseon, combining an emphasis on study and learning with moral attainment and an orientation towards social order. For the noble literati, the seowon were institutions where scholars could elaborate upon Confucian ideas and craft an enlightened ethos of moral rule. Seowon even had the power to petition the king if they perceived an issue that needed addressing. With their emphasis on local and national education, these scholars cultivated links of mentorship and scholarship that became powerful forces. But politics is a messy business, and seowon faced a bitter division on the subject of tradition versus reform, kingly glory versus civil morality.

The philosophy of Neo-Confucianism – Seongnihak – was central to Joseon society. Based on what in Chinese is the Cheng Zhu school of Neo-Confucianism, it emphasized the purity of moral principles (li), which were bound to become corrupted by material forces and realities. The role of the Confucian scholar, then, was to conduct philosophical and scientific inquiry and analysis to identify, purify, and then render li into reality, or at least as best one could.

Seonbi refers to a class and category of Confucian scholars during Goryeo and Joseon who laid aside the temptations of power and wealth in order to educate and advance the public. These could provide an important check to royal power, especially given that seonbi could petition the ruler, muster military groups, or had practiced archery (considered a philosophical art in Joseon), and many suffered for being seen to have overstepped their bounds. Yet the role of the independent scholar was a crucial part of Joseon, and a way that society maintained an air of stability, providing a check to rulers that sought to consolidate power for their own advantage.

The Gyeongguk Daejeon was the great code of law, composed in Goryeo but serving as the basis for Joseon political norms. Finally completed in 1485, it contained 319 provisions. It set up the ministries of Joseon, providing separate administration for civic personnel, taxation, religious rites, military, justice, and public works, and remained the foundational text for Joseon law and society.

Joseon culture was founded upon the samgang, three fundamental principles: loyalty to the monarch, obedience to parents, and a divide between men and women. The samgang led to a stable but hierarchical society, where one’s place and duties were always clear. Korean society was split, too, into different social classes – the yangban (nobility), the sangmin (regular commoners), and chonmin (lower castes, such as butchers, shamans and enslaved people).

The Joseon monarchy focused on stability, balancing competing interests between noble families, Confucian groups, and the threat of foreign wars and popular uprisings. This was especially the case under King Jeongjo (r. 1776-1800), who engaged in a series of reforms aimed at greater cultural, military, and political security. Part of this process involved the creation of the Royal Elite Guard, the Jangyongyoung.

Elite troops traditionally drawn from the ranks of the nobility present a problem – how much do they serve the monarch, and how much do they serve their particular lord? In contrast, the Jangyongyoung brought promising commoners into intensive training in firearms, martial arts, and discipline, and created a corps that would have Joseon, not a particular clan, as their primary patron. Evidentially, the corps worked: from their establishment to Joseon’s fall 200 years later, the kingdom was at peace.

The turtle ship, the geobukseon, was a kind of protected warship used throughout Joseon. 19th century turtle ships were almost completely covered in order to repel boarders, complete with spikes and spines possibly made of iron, though the weight of metal might have been prohibitive. Some of these ships were armed with cannon, some had fire-arrows, and some were mounted with a terrifying dragon’s head, so as to deploy fear, as well as fire, as a weapon.

Admiral Yi Sun-sin deployed turtle ships in his defense of Joseon in the Imjin wars, and it was in his period that they reached their height. While they were still present in the Korean navy into the 19th century, after which Joseon’s navy declined to nearly nonexistent, later mechanized craft would prove more effective.

"He who learns but does not think is lost. He who thinks but does not learn is endangered."
"Of all the things in the world, humanity is the most precious."
"A miserly father always has a wastrel son; an intelligent wife, a stupid husband. This is the way of things, so I laugh by myself. But nobody knows."
"The ruler sees his subjects as his hands and feet. The subjects see him as their head."

As empires rise and fall, Joseon persists. In the calm behind its fleets of turtle ships, Joseon builds a society that balances Confucian meritocracy and kingship, a harmonious order as all else seems to fall. Hold the line, stand firm, and let Joseon thrive.
Joseon has a unique statistic called City Limit. This is literally a limit on the number of Settlements that can be turned into Cities, so plan carefully!
As Joseon, complete 4 Cultural or Expansionist Minor Triumphs in a single Apex Age.
Contains a new Modern Age Civilization, Joseon.
The good doctor leaves the shade of the ginkgo tree and enters the grounds of the seowon, drawn by its mingling of intellectual and spiritual energies. Where to even begin?
Converse with the scholars in the pagoda.
Pay respects to the departed at the shrine.

The son of a disgraced nobleman arrives at Hwaesong, hoping to use the formidable setting to rehabilitate his family's legacy. Among his retinue of 1,800 servants, attendants and guards, there are painters instructed to capture the grandeur of the visit, but it is impossible to portray every lavish event.
Depict his generosity with his mother's birthday banquet.
Convey his strict standards with the special civil service exams.
Prove the loyalty he commands with military exercises.
A faction of sarim has been creating a stir in the capital, questioning the ruling elite's power and advocating for the common people's voices to be heard.
Hear what they have to say.
Set all your hearts on learning, not petty squabbles.

After a faction of literati has been expelled from {1_Capital}, stability returns to the capital. But the purged sarim have established a seowon in the countryside, where their ideas begin to spread anew.
Pay the sarim no mind – they are no longer a threat.

Sworn to protect the heart of the empire, all jangyongyoung study the twenty-four martial arts set down in the official military manuals. Each must be prepared for any eventuality, but certain techniques become favored among the guards.
With a dragon's head that breathes fire and a hull studded with spikes, the new ship claims its first victim, proving out its bold design. Another monster prowls the seas.
{1_reward} and {2_reward} Turtle Ships, but all new Turtle Ships start with 50 Damage.
Let our bravest crews sail the kobukson.
{1_reward} on Turtle Ships, but Turtle Ships have +50% Maintenance.
With Yi Sun-sin's leadership, the fleet will know no equal.
A Fleet Commander with 2 Promotions and 4 Turtle Ships.

In their first meeting, it is difficult to tell who is more shocked: the foreign delegation, at the revelation that their hosts do not in fact have ears on their elbows; or Korean officials, at the notion that such is their portrayal abroad.
The world must know the true Joseon.
Let others think what they may.
The Illustrated Conduct provides a new source of moral instruction for literate and illiterate Koreans alike. If one is true to one's bonds, a peaceful and harmonious heaven awaits.
Make it required reading for the state exams.
Ensure it is circulated in the provinces.

Of the thirty-three students who are allowed to pass the Gwageo examination every three years, thirty-two have been chosen to enter civil service. Only two pupils have proved themselves worthy to be the thirty-third: one, the youngest in a long line of sajok, and the other, a yangin from a remote farming town.
Let the sajok take his rightful place.
Grant the yangin a chance to prove himself.
A great number of local markets have begun to operate outside the purview of the state. These jangsi are too profitable to be ignored, but are unlikely to bow to government authority.
Leave them be; they know what they are doing.
Literacy in the Korean domain booms, but to bring wisdom to all the masses, printing houses require many thousands of pieces of movable type. Thousands of tiny, tiny metal pieces.
Surely there are better uses for these resources.

The emissary arrives before the Joseon court, his waxed moustache barely moving as he smiles. His Korean is understandable, but hardly polite as he gestures for his porters to reveal crates of gifts. “Take a look! There are far more wonders than these should you open your lands to us.”

The administrator of {1_Capital} presents a new urban plan, lines of market squares, boulevards, gates and walls elaborately detailed with careful brushwork. The court geomancer steps up, and with one brushstroke, draws other lines: wind and water, the flow of ki from the mountains and rivers.
